case_info.scenario: A 30-year-old nulliparous woman with migraines, depression, and obesity (12.7-kg [28-lb] weight gain over the prior 2 years) presented to the primary care clinic with 1 month of daily headaches, transient bilateral blurry vision, and persistent vision loss in the temporal region of the right eye. She experienced right-sided temporal and frontal headaches accompanied by intermittent auditory hissing, without auras. The headaches lasted for several hours each day, worsened when she was lying flat, and were temporarily relieved by acetaminophen. She took no daily medications or supplements but had a contraceptive etonogestrel implant that had been placed 9 months prior to presentation. Her temperature was 37.1 °C (98.8 °F); heart rate, 95/min; blood pressure, 106/70 mm Hg; height, 1.57 m (5 ft 2 in); weight, 113.9 kg (251 lb); and body mass index, 45 (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters). Her pupillary reflexes were brisk bilaterally, without a relative afferent pupillary defect. By visual field testing to confrontation, she had a temporal visual field defect in the right eye. Her physical examination findings were otherwise normal. The patient was referred for same-day ophthalmology evaluation, which revealed visual acuity of 20/20 bilaterally and normal extraocular movements without nystagmus or ocular misalignment. Mild bilateral papilledema was seen on dilated fundoscopy (Figure). Automated visual field testing demonstrated enlargement of the physiologic (temporal) blind spot in the right eye and mild constriction of the left nasal visual field.

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that symptoms of positional headache, visual blurring, and pulsatile tinnitus are characteristic of IIH in a female with obesity. Lumbar puncture (choice B) should not be performed until neuroimaging has confirmed absence of an intracranial lesion causing papilledema. Prednisone (choice C) is incorrect because the patient’s symptoms were not characteristic of optic neuritis or temporal arteritis. Removal of the birth control implant (choice D) is not recommended because there is no known association between hormonal contraception and IIH.1 IIH is a condition of elevated intracranial pressure without a known cause. It is diagnosed using the modified Dandy criteria, which include (1) symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure such as headache, tinnitus, diplopia, and/or visual disturbances without secondary etiologies (eg, intracranial tumors, venous sinus thrombosis, infection, or medications such as vitamin A derivatives, tetracyclines, lithium, and human growth hormone); (2) papilledema on fundus examination; and (3) elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure on lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position (opening pressure >25 cm H2O in adults; >28 cm H2O in children). IIH primarily affects women of childbearing age and is strongly associated with obesity.2A cross-sectional study of 85 million US patients reported that the prevalence of IIH increased from 7.3 individuals per 100 000 in 2015 to 9.9 per 100 000 in 2022,3correlating with increasing US obesity rates. The pathogenesis of IIH is unclear but may involve hypersecretion and/or decreased absorption of cerebrospinal fluid related to increased levels of androgens, glucocorticoids, glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), and inflammatory cytokines associated with central adiposity.4 First-line treatment for IIH is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (eg, acetazolamide), which causes a rapid reduction of intracranial pressure through decreased cerebrospinal fluid production. Patients with suspected IIH may be treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor before confirmation of papilledema, if ophthalmologic examination cannot be not performed expeditiously. If brain MRI/MRV shows no intracranial lesions, patients with suspected IIH should undergo a diagnostic lumbar puncture to determine if cerebrospinal fluid pressure is elevated. While lumbar puncture temporarily decreases intracranial pressure by removing cerebrospinal fluid and may relieve IIH symptoms in the short term, it is not definitive therapy. The combination of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and weight loss (5%-10%) is effective at improving peripheral vision, papilledema, and vision-related quality-of-life measures.5Small randomized trials of bariatric surgery and a GLP-1 receptor agonist (exenatide) in patients with IIH have demonstrated decreased intracranial pressure compared with control patients.6,7Patients with IIH and fulminant vision loss, or those whose symptoms do not improve or worsen despite medical therapy, may require emergent ventriculoperitoneal shunting, optic nerve sheath fenestration, or venous sinus stenting, although evidence for efficacy of surgical options is lacking.8 The visual prognosis of patients with IIH depends on papilledema grade and visual symptom severity at diagnosis.9,10Untreated IIH can lead to permanent vision loss within several weeks, so early symptom recognition and treatment are important to avoid blindness. Serial ophthalmologic evaluation every 1 to 3 months with quantitative optical coherence tomography and automated visual field testing is indicated for all patients with IIH who have papilledema to evaluate response to therapy and guide treatment. Brain MRI/MRV performed on the day of presentation revealed no intracranial abnormalities but demonstrated diminutive transverse venous sinuses and prominent optic nerve sheath fluid bilaterally, suggestive of elevated intracranial pressure. Same-day lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position revealed a cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure of 33 cm H2O (reference, ≤25 cm H2O); examination of the cerebrospinal fluid showed normal levels of glucose and total protein and no pleocytosis. The patient was prescribed acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and was encouraged to exercise and make dietary modifications. At 1-month follow-up, she reported near-complete resolution of visual blurring and headaches and had lost 2.27 kg (5 lb). Ophthalmologic examination revealed no residual disc edema or visual field defects. She was advised to continue acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and to continue weight loss efforts.

per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing

worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

1. Mental Demand

   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

   Definition:

     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more

[Clinical case]
A 30-year-old nulliparous woman with migraines, depression, and obesity (12.7-kg [28-lb] weight gain over the prior 2 years) presented to the primary care clinic with 1 month of daily headaches, transient bilateral blurry vision, and persistent vision loss in the temporal region of the right eye. She experienced right-sided temporal and frontal headaches accompanied by intermittent auditory hissing, without auras. The headaches lasted for several hours each day, worsened when she was lying flat, and were temporarily relieved by acetaminophen. She took no daily medications or supplements but had a contraceptive etonogestrel implant that had been placed 9 months prior to presentation. Her temperature was 37.1 °C (98.8 °F); heart rate, 95/min; blood pressure, 106/70 mm Hg; height, 1.57 m (5 ft 2 in); weight, 113.9 kg (251 lb); and body mass index, 45 (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters). Her pupillary reflexes were brisk bilaterally, without a relative afferent pupillary defect. By visual field testing to confrontation, she had a temporal visual field defect in the right eye. Her physical examination findings were otherwise normal. The patient was referred for same-day ophthalmology evaluation, which revealed visual acuity of 20/20 bilaterally and normal extraocular movements without nystagmus or ocular misalignment. Mild bilateral papilledema was seen on dilated fundoscopy (Figure). Automated visual field testing demonstrated enlargement of the physiologic (temporal) blind spot in the right eye and mild constriction of the left nasal visual field.

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that symptoms of positional headache, visual blurring, and pulsatile tinnitus are characteristic of IIH in a female with obesity. Lumbar puncture (choice B) should not be performed until neuroimaging has confirmed absence of an intracranial lesion causing papilledema. Prednisone (choice C) is incorrect because the patient’s symptoms were not characteristic of optic neuritis or temporal arteritis. Removal of the birth control implant (choice D) is not recommended because there is no known association between hormonal contraception and IIH.1 IIH is a condition of elevated intracranial pressure without a known cause. It is diagnosed using the modified Dandy criteria, which include (1) symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure such as headache, tinnitus, diplopia, and/or visual disturbances without secondary etiologies (eg, intracranial tumors, venous sinus thrombosis, infection, or medications such as vitamin A derivatives, tetracyclines, lithium, and human growth hormone); (2) papilledema on fundus examination; and (3) elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure on lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position (opening pressure >25 cm H2O in adults; >28 cm H2O in children). IIH primarily affects women of childbearing age and is strongly associated with obesity.2A cross-sectional study of 85 million US patients reported that the prevalence of IIH increased from 7.3 individuals per 100 000 in 2015 to 9.9 per 100 000 in 2022,3correlating with increasing US obesity rates. The pathogenesis of IIH is unclear but may involve hypersecretion and/or decreased absorption of cerebrospinal fluid related to increased levels of androgens, glucocorticoids, glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), and inflammatory cytokines associated with central adiposity.4 First-line treatment for IIH is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (eg, acetazolamide), which causes a rapid reduction of intracranial pressure through decreased cerebrospinal fluid production. Patients with suspected IIH may be treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor before confirmation of papilledema, if ophthalmologic examination cannot be not performed expeditiously. If brain MRI/MRV shows no intracranial lesions, patients with suspected IIH should undergo a diagnostic lumbar puncture to determine if cerebrospinal fluid pressure is elevated. While lumbar puncture temporarily decreases intracranial pressure by removing cerebrospinal fluid and may relieve IIH symptoms in the short term, it is not definitive therapy. The combination of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and weight loss (5%-10%) is effective at improving peripheral vision, papilledema, and vision-related quality-of-life measures.5Small randomized trials of bariatric surgery and a GLP-1 receptor agonist (exenatide) in patients with IIH have demonstrated decreased intracranial pressure compared with control patients.6,7Patients with IIH and fulminant vision loss, or those whose symptoms do not improve or worsen despite medical therapy, may require emergent ventriculoperitoneal shunting, optic nerve sheath fenestration, or venous sinus stenting, although evidence for efficacy of surgical options is lacking.8 The visual prognosis of patients with IIH depends on papilledema grade and visual symptom severity at diagnosis.9,10Untreated IIH can lead to permanent vision loss within several weeks, so early symptom recognition and treatment are important to avoid blindness. Serial ophthalmologic evaluation every 1 to 3 months with quantitative optical coherence tomography and automated visual field testing is indicated for all patients with IIH who have papilledema to evaluate response to therapy and guide treatment. Brain MRI/MRV performed on the day of presentation revealed no intracranial abnormalities but demonstrated diminutive transverse venous sinuses and prominent optic nerve sheath fluid bilaterally, suggestive of elevated intracranial pressure. Same-day lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position revealed a cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure of 33 cm H2O (reference, ≤25 cm H2O); examination of the cerebrospinal fluid showed normal levels of glucose and total protein and no pleocytosis. The patient was prescribed acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and was encouraged to exercise and make dietary modifications. At 1-month follow-up, she reported near-complete resolution of visual blurring and headaches and had lost 2.27 kg (5 lb). Ophthalmologic examination revealed no residual disc edema or visual field defects. She was advised to continue acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and to continue weight loss efforts.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that symptoms of positional headache, visual blurring, and pulsatile tinnitus are characteristic of IIH in a female with obesity. Lumbar puncture (choice B) should not be performed until neuroimaging has confirmed absence of an intracranial lesion causing papilledema. Prednisone (choice C) is incorrect because the patient’s symptoms were not characteristic of optic neuritis or temporal arteritis. Removal of the birth control implant (choice D) is not recommended because there is no known association between hormonal contraception and IIH.1 IIH is a condition of elevated intracranial pressure without a known cause. It is diagnosed using the modified Dandy criteria, which include (1) symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure such as headache, tinnitus, diplopia, and/or visual disturbances without secondary etiologies (eg, intracranial tumors, venous sinus thrombosis, infection, or medications such as vitamin A derivatives, tetracyclines, lithium, and human growth hormone); (2) papilledema on fundus examination; and (3) elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure on lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position (opening pressure >25 cm H2O in adults; >28 cm H2O in children). IIH primarily affects women of childbearing age and is strongly associated with obesity.2A cross-sectional study of 85 million US patients reported that the prevalence of IIH increased from 7.3 individuals per 100 000 in 2015 to 9.9 per 100 000 in 2022,3correlating with increasing US obesity rates. The pathogenesis of IIH is unclear but may involve hypersecretion and/or decreased absorption of cerebrospinal fluid related to increased levels of androgens, glucocorticoids, glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), and inflammatory cytokines associated with central adiposity.4 First-line treatment for IIH is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (eg, acetazolamide), which causes a rapid reduction of intracranial pressure through decreased cerebrospinal fluid production. Patients with suspected IIH may be treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor before confirmation of papilledema, if ophthalmologic examination cannot be not performed expeditiously. If brain MRI/MRV shows no intracranial lesions, patients with suspected IIH should undergo a diagnostic lumbar puncture to determine if cerebrospinal fluid pressure is elevated. While lumbar puncture temporarily decreases intracranial pressure by removing cerebrospinal fluid and may relieve IIH symptoms in the short term, it is not definitive therapy. The combination of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and weight loss (5%-10%) is effective at improving peripheral vision, papilledema, and vision-related quality-of-life measures.5Small randomized trials of bariatric surgery and a GLP-1 receptor agonist (exenatide) in patients with IIH have demonstrated decreased intracranial pressure compared with control patients.6,7Patients with IIH and fulminant vision loss, or those whose symptoms do not improve or worsen despite medical therapy, may require emergent ventriculoperitoneal shunting, optic nerve sheath fenestration, or venous sinus stenting, although evidence for efficacy of surgical options is lacking.8 The visual prognosis of patients with IIH depends on papilledema grade and visual symptom severity at diagnosis.9,10Untreated IIH can lead to permanent vision loss within several weeks, so early symptom recognition and treatment are important to avoid blindness. Serial ophthalmologic evaluation every 1 to 3 months with quantitative optical coherence tomography and automated visual field testing is indicated for all patients with IIH who have papilledema to evaluate response to therapy and guide treatment. Brain MRI/MRV performed on the day of presentation revealed no intracranial abnormalities but demonstrated diminutive transverse venous sinuses and prominent optic nerve sheath fluid bilaterally, suggestive of elevated intracranial pressure. Same-day lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position revealed a cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure of 33 cm H2O (reference, ≤25 cm H2O); examination of the cerebrospinal fluid showed normal levels of glucose and total protein and no pleocytosis. The patient was prescribed acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and was encouraged to exercise and make dietary modifications. At 1-month follow-up, she reported near-complete resolution of visual blurring and headaches and had lost 2.27 kg (5 lb). Ophthalmologic examination revealed no residual disc edema or visual field defects. She was advised to continue acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and to continue weight loss efforts.

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that symptoms of positional headache, visual blurring, and pulsatile tinnitus are characteristic of IIH in a female with obesity. Lumbar puncture (choice B) should not be performed until neuroimaging has confirmed absence of an intracranial lesion causing papilledema. Prednisone (choice C) is incorrect because the patient’s symptoms were not characteristic of optic neuritis or temporal arteritis. Removal of the birth control implant (choice D) is not recommended because there is no known association between hormonal contraception and IIH.1 IIH is a condition of elevated intracranial pressure without a known cause. It is diagnosed using the modified Dandy criteria, which include (1) symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure such as headache, tinnitus, diplopia, and/or visual disturbances without secondary etiologies (eg, intracranial tumors, venous sinus thrombosis, infection, or medications such as vitamin A derivatives, tetracyclines, lithium, and human growth hormone); (2) papilledema on fundus examination; and (3) elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure on lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position (opening pressure >25 cm H2O in adults; >28 cm H2O in children). IIH primarily affects women of childbearing age and is strongly associated with obesity.2A cross-sectional study of 85 million US patients reported that the prevalence of IIH increased from 7.3 individuals per 100 000 in 2015 to 9.9 per 100 000 in 2022,3correlating with increasing US obesity rates. The pathogenesis of IIH is unclear but may involve hypersecretion and/or decreased absorption of cerebrospinal fluid related to increased levels of androgens, glucocorticoids, glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), and inflammatory cytokines associated with central adiposity.4 First-line treatment for IIH is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (eg, acetazolamide), which causes a rapid reduction of intracranial pressure through decreased cerebrospinal fluid production. Patients with suspected IIH may be treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor before confirmation of papilledema, if ophthalmologic examination cannot be not performed expeditiously. If brain MRI/MRV shows no intracranial lesions, patients with suspected IIH should undergo a diagnostic lumbar puncture to determine if cerebrospinal fluid pressure is elevated. While lumbar puncture temporarily decreases intracranial pressure by removing cerebrospinal fluid and may relieve IIH symptoms in the short term, it is not definitive therapy. The combination of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and weight loss (5%-10%) is effective at improving peripheral vision, papilledema, and vision-related quality-of-life measures.5Small randomized trials of bariatric surgery and a GLP-1 receptor agonist (exenatide) in patients with IIH have demonstrated decreased intracranial pressure compared with control patients.6,7Patients with IIH and fulminant vision loss, or those whose symptoms do not improve or worsen despite medical therapy, may require emergent ventriculoperitoneal shunting, optic nerve sheath fenestration, or venous sinus stenting, although evidence for efficacy of surgical options is lacking.8 The visual prognosis of patients with IIH depends on papilledema grade and visual symptom severity at diagnosis.9,10Untreated IIH can lead to permanent vision loss within several weeks, so early symptom recognition and treatment are important to avoid blindness. Serial ophthalmologic evaluation every 1 to 3 months with quantitative optical coherence tomography and automated visual field testing is indicated for all patients with IIH who have papilledema to evaluate response to therapy and guide treatment. Brain MRI/MRV performed on the day of presentation revealed no intracranial abnormalities but demonstrated diminutive transverse venous sinuses and prominent optic nerve sheath fluid bilaterally, suggestive of elevated intracranial pressure. Same-day lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position revealed a cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure of 33 cm H2O (reference, ≤25 cm H2O); examination of the cerebrospinal fluid showed normal levels of glucose and total protein and no pleocytosis. The patient was prescribed acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and was encouraged to exercise and make dietary modifications. At 1-month follow-up, she reported near-complete resolution of visual blurring and headaches and had lost 2.27 kg (5 lb). Ophthalmologic examination revealed no residual disc edema or visual field defects. She was advised to continue acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and to continue weight loss efforts.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that symptoms of positional headache, visual blurring, and pulsatile tinnitus are characteristic of IIH in a female with obesity. Lumbar puncture (choice B) should not be performed until neuroimaging has confirmed absence of an intracranial lesion causing papilledema. Prednisone (choice C) is incorrect because the patient’s symptoms were not characteristic of optic neuritis or temporal arteritis. Removal of the birth control implant (choice D) is not recommended because there is no known association between hormonal contraception and IIH.1 IIH is a condition of elevated intracranial pressure without a known cause. It is diagnosed using the modified Dandy criteria, which include (1) symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure such as headache, tinnitus, diplopia, and/or visual disturbances without secondary etiologies (eg, intracranial tumors, venous sinus thrombosis, infection, or medications such as vitamin A derivatives, tetracyclines, lithium, and human growth hormone); (2) papilledema on fundus examination; and (3) elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure on lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position (opening pressure >25 cm H2O in adults; >28 cm H2O in children). IIH primarily affects women of childbearing age and is strongly associated with obesity.2A cross-sectional study of 85 million US patients reported that the prevalence of IIH increased from 7.3 individuals per 100 000 in 2015 to 9.9 per 100 000 in 2022,3correlating with increasing US obesity rates. The pathogenesis of IIH is unclear but may involve hypersecretion and/or decreased absorption of cerebrospinal fluid related to increased levels of androgens, glucocorticoids, glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), and inflammatory cytokines associated with central adiposity.4 First-line treatment for IIH is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (eg, acetazolamide), which causes a rapid reduction of intracranial pressure through decreased cerebrospinal fluid production. Patients with suspected IIH may be treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor before confirmation of papilledema, if ophthalmologic examination cannot be not performed expeditiously. If brain MRI/MRV shows no intracranial lesions, patients with suspected IIH should undergo a diagnostic lumbar puncture to determine if cerebrospinal fluid pressure is elevated. While lumbar puncture temporarily decreases intracranial pressure by removing cerebrospinal fluid and may relieve IIH symptoms in the short term, it is not definitive therapy. The combination of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and weight loss (5%-10%) is effective at improving peripheral vision, papilledema, and vision-related quality-of-life measures.5Small randomized trials of bariatric surgery and a GLP-1 receptor agonist (exenatide) in patients with IIH have demonstrated decreased intracranial pressure compared with control patients.6,7Patients with IIH and fulminant vision loss, or those whose symptoms do not improve or worsen despite medical therapy, may require emergent ventriculoperitoneal shunting, optic nerve sheath fenestration, or venous sinus stenting, although evidence for efficacy of surgical options is lacking.8 The visual prognosis of patients with IIH depends on papilledema grade and visual symptom severity at diagnosis.9,10Untreated IIH can lead to permanent vision loss within several weeks, so early symptom recognition and treatment are important to avoid blindness. Serial ophthalmologic evaluation every 1 to 3 months with quantitative optical coherence tomography and automated visual field testing is indicated for all patients with IIH who have papilledema to evaluate response to therapy and guide treatment. Brain MRI/MRV performed on the day of presentation revealed no intracranial abnormalities but demonstrated diminutive transverse venous sinuses and prominent optic nerve sheath fluid bilaterally, suggestive of elevated intracranial pressure. Same-day lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position revealed a cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure of 33 cm H2O (reference, ≤25 cm H2O); examination of the cerebrospinal fluid showed normal levels of glucose and total protein and no pleocytosis. The patient was prescribed acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and was encouraged to exercise and make dietary modifications. At 1-month follow-up, she reported near-complete resolution of visual blurring and headaches and had lost 2.27 kg (5 lb). Ophthalmologic examination revealed no residual disc edema or visual field defects. She was advised to continue acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and to continue weight loss efforts.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that symptoms of positional headache, visual blurring, and pulsatile tinnitus are characteristic of IIH in a female with obesity. Lumbar puncture (choice B) should not be performed until neuroimaging has confirmed absence of an intracranial lesion causing papilledema. Prednisone (choice C) is incorrect because the patient’s symptoms were not characteristic of optic neuritis or temporal arteritis. Removal of the birth control implant (choice D) is not recommended because there is no known association between hormonal contraception and IIH.1 IIH is a condition of elevated intracranial pressure without a known cause. It is diagnosed using the modified Dandy criteria, which include (1) symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure such as headache, tinnitus, diplopia, and/or visual disturbances without secondary etiologies (eg, intracranial tumors, venous sinus thrombosis, infection, or medications such as vitamin A derivatives, tetracyclines, lithium, and human growth hormone); (2) papilledema on fundus examination; and (3) elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure on lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position (opening pressure >25 cm H2O in adults; >28 cm H2O in children). IIH primarily affects women of childbearing age and is strongly associated with obesity.2A cross-sectional study of 85 million US patients reported that the prevalence of IIH increased from 7.3 individuals per 100 000 in 2015 to 9.9 per 100 000 in 2022,3correlating with increasing US obesity rates. The pathogenesis of IIH is unclear but may involve hypersecretion and/or decreased absorption of cerebrospinal fluid related to increased levels of androgens, glucocorticoids, glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), and inflammatory cytokines associated with central adiposity.4 First-line treatment for IIH is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (eg, acetazolamide), which causes a rapid reduction of intracranial pressure through decreased cerebrospinal fluid production. Patients with suspected IIH may be treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor before confirmation of papilledema, if ophthalmologic examination cannot be not performed expeditiously. If brain MRI/MRV shows no intracranial lesions, patients with suspected IIH should undergo a diagnostic lumbar puncture to determine if cerebrospinal fluid pressure is elevated. While lumbar puncture temporarily decreases intracranial pressure by removing cerebrospinal fluid and may relieve IIH symptoms in the short term, it is not definitive therapy. 2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that symptoms of positional headache, visual blurring, and pulsatile tinnitus are characteristic of IIH in a female with obesity. Lumbar puncture (choice B) should not be performed until neuroimaging has confirmed absence of an intracranial lesion causing papilledema. Prednisone (choice C) is incorrect because the patient’s symptoms were not characteristic of optic neuritis or temporal arteritis. Removal of the birth control implant (choice D) is not recommended because there is no known association between hormonal contraception and IIH.1 IIH is a condition of elevated intracranial pressure without a known cause. It is diagnosed using the modified Dandy criteria, which include (1) symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure such as headache, tinnitus, diplopia, and/or visual disturbances without secondary etiologies (eg, intracranial tumors, venous sinus thrombosis, infection, or medications such as vitamin A derivatives, tetracyclines, lithium, and human growth hormone); (2) papilledema on fundus examination; and (3) elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure on lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position (opening pressure >25 cm H2O in adults; >28 cm H2O in children). IIH primarily affects women of childbearing age and is strongly associated with obesity.2A cross-sectional study of 85 million US patients reported that the prevalence of IIH increased from 7.3 individuals per 100 000 in 2015 to 9.9 per 100 000 in 2022,3correlating with increasing US obesity rates. The pathogenesis of IIH is unclear but may involve hypersecretion and/or decreased absorption of cerebrospinal fluid related to increased levels of androgens, glucocorticoids, glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), and inflammatory cytokines associated with central adiposity.4 First-line treatment for IIH is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (eg, acetazolamide), which causes a rapid reduction of intracranial pressure through decreased cerebrospinal fluid production. Patients with suspected IIH may be treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor before confirmation of papilledema, if ophthalmologic examination cannot be not performed expeditiously. If brain MRI/MRV shows no intracranial lesions, patients with suspected IIH should undergo a diagnostic lumbar puncture to determine if cerebrospinal fluid pressure is elevated. While lumbar puncture temporarily decreases intracranial pressure by removing cerebrospinal fluid and may relieve IIH symptoms in the short term, it is not definitive therapy. The combination of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and weight loss (5%-10%) is effective at improving peripheral vision, papilledema, and vision-related quality-of-life measures.5Small randomized trials of bariatric surgery and a GLP-1 receptor agonist (exenatide) in patients with IIH have demonstrated decreased intracranial pressure compared with control patients.6,7Patients with IIH and fulminant vision loss, or those whose symptoms do not improve or worsen despite medical therapy, may require emergent ventriculoperitoneal shunting, optic nerve sheath fenestration, or venous sinus stenting, although evidence for efficacy of surgical options is lacking.8 The visual prognosis of patients with IIH depends on papilledema grade and visual symptom severity at diagnosis.9,10Untreated IIH can lead to permanent vision loss within several weeks, so early symptom recognition and treatment are important to avoid blindness. Serial ophthalmologic evaluation every 1 to 3 months with quantitative optical coherence tomography and automated visual field testing is indicated for all patients with IIH who have papilledema to evaluate response to therapy and guide treatment. Brain MRI/MRV performed on the day of presentation revealed no intracranial abnormalities but demonstrated diminutive transverse venous sinuses and prominent optic nerve sheath fluid bilaterally, suggestive of elevated intracranial pressure. Same-day lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position revealed a cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure of 33 cm H2O (reference, ≤25 cm H2O); examination of the cerebrospinal fluid showed normal levels of glucose and total protein and no pleocytosis. The patient was prescribed acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and was encouraged to exercise and make dietary modifications. At 1-month follow-up, she reported near-complete resolution of visual blurring and headaches and had lost 2.27 kg (5 lb). Ophthalmologic examination revealed no residual disc edema or visual field defects. She was advised to continue acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and to continue weight loss efforts.

4. Frustration

case_info.explanation: A. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that symptoms of positional headache, visual blurring, and pulsatile tinnitus are characteristic of IIH in a female with obesity. Lumbar puncture (choice B) should not be performed until neuroimaging has confirmed absence of an intracranial lesion causing papilledema. Prednisone (choice C) is incorrect because the patient’s symptoms were not characteristic of optic neuritis or temporal arteritis. Removal of the birth control implant (choice D) is not recommended because there is no known association between hormonal contraception and IIH.1 IIH is a condition of elevated intracranial pressure without a known cause. It is diagnosed using the modified Dandy criteria, which include (1) symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure such as headache, tinnitus, diplopia, and/or visual disturbances without secondary etiologies (eg, intracranial tumors, venous sinus thrombosis, infection, or medications such as vitamin A derivatives, tetracyclines, lithium, and human growth hormone); (2) papilledema on fundus examination; and (3) elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure on lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position (opening pressure >25 cm H2O in adults; >28 cm H2O in children). IIH primarily affects women of childbearing age and is strongly associated with obesity.2A cross-sectional study of 85 million US patients reported that the prevalence of IIH increased from 7.3 individuals per 100 000 in 2015 to 9.9 per 100 000 in 2022,3correlating with increasing US obesity rates. The pathogenesis of IIH is unclear but may involve hypersecretion and/or decreased absorption of cerebrospinal fluid related to increased levels of androgens, glucocorticoids, glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), and inflammatory cytokines associated with central adiposity.4 First-line treatment for IIH is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (eg, acetazolamide), which causes a rapid reduction of intracranial pressure through decreased cerebrospinal fluid production. Patients with suspected IIH may be treated with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor before confirmation of papilledema, if ophthalmologic examination cannot be not performed expeditiously. If brain MRI/MRV shows no intracranial lesions, patients with suspected IIH should undergo a diagnostic lumbar puncture to determine if cerebrospinal fluid pressure is elevated. While lumbar puncture temporarily decreases intracranial pressure by removing cerebrospinal fluid and may relieve IIH symptoms in the short term, it is not definitive therapy. The combination of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and weight loss (5%-10%) is effective at improving peripheral vision, papilledema, and vision-related quality-of-life measures.5Small randomized trials of bariatric surgery and a GLP-1 receptor agonist (exenatide) in patients with IIH have demonstrated decreased intracranial pressure compared with control patients.6,7Patients with IIH and fulminant vision loss, or those whose symptoms do not improve or worsen despite medical therapy, may require emergent ventriculoperitoneal shunting, optic nerve sheath fenestration, or venous sinus stenting, although evidence for efficacy of surgical options is lacking.8 The visual prognosis of patients with IIH depends on papilledema grade and visual symptom severity at diagnosis.9,10Untreated IIH can lead to permanent vision loss within several weeks, so early symptom recognition and treatment are important to avoid blindness. Serial ophthalmologic evaluation every 1 to 3 months with quantitative optical coherence tomography and automated visual field testing is indicated for all patients with IIH who have papilledema to evaluate response to therapy and guide treatment. Brain MRI/MRV performed on the day of presentation revealed no intracranial abnormalities but demonstrated diminutive transverse venous sinuses and prominent optic nerve sheath fluid bilaterally, suggestive of elevated intracranial pressure. Same-day lumbar puncture performed in the lateral decubitus position revealed a cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure of 33 cm H2O (reference, ≤25 cm H2O); examination of the cerebrospinal fluid showed normal levels of glucose and total protein and no pleocytosis. The patient was prescribed acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and was encouraged to exercise and make dietary modifications. At 1-month follow-up, she reported near-complete resolution of visual blurring and headaches and had lost 2.27 kg (5 lb). Ophthalmologic examination revealed no residual disc edema or visual field defects. She was advised to continue acetazolamide (500 mg 3 times daily) and to continue weight loss efforts.
